segments.text: Watch a pulse of light, just a few wave cycles long, race along a silicon wire toward a tiny ring.
Some of it hops into the ring, circles around and around, and leaks back out a little on every lap.
Every model so far was an approximation. This is Maxwell's equations themselves, solved on a grid. How?
It's called finite-difference time-domain, FDTD, and it rests on two ideas: leapfrogging fields, and a border made of complex numbers.
In two dimensions, the electric field E points straight out of the screen, and the magnetic field H lies flat in the plane.
Maxwell's equations then say two things: a changing H is driven by the curl of E, and a changing E by the curl of H.
The curl measures swirl: how much a field circulates around each point.
Watch a bump of E. Its slopes make H start to circulate around it.
That swirling H lowers E in the middle and raises it around the edge. The bump spreads into a ring: a wave that pushes itself along.
These rules contain only derivatives, which compare each point with its neighbours. Everything is local.
On a computer, sample the fields on a grid, and replace each derivative by a difference of neighbours.
But that difference, divided by the spacing, gives the slope best at the midpoint between the samples, not at either end.
So in 1966, Kane Yee put H exactly at those midpoints: half a cell away from E.
Time gets the same trick: E lives on whole time steps, and H on the half steps in between.
The algorithm is a leapfrog. Use the curl of E to update H, then the curl of H to update E, and repeat.
Here it is in 1D, with real numbers: each new value uses only its two neighbours, yet the pulse marches on.
Matter is just one number per cell, the permittivity ε. Any shape you can paint on the grid, you can simulate.
The grid has two rules of its own. First, a speed limit: each step, news travels only to neighbouring cells, so it spreads in a diamond.
Light spreads in a circle, which must fit inside the diamond: in 2D, c Δt ≤ Δx/√2. This is the Courant limit.
Break it by just six percent, and the computed field explodes.
Second, the grid distorts waves. Recall the k-circle: in free space, all directions share one wavelength.
On the grid, the circle bulges, most along the axes: short waves travel too slowly, slowest along the grid lines.
A pulse becomes a squarish ring, trailed by ripples. The fix: ten to twenty cells per wavelength, or more.
Now the hardest part: the grid must end somewhere, but real light just keeps going.
If the grid simply stops, its edge acts as a mirror, and the echo ruins the answer.
So add a layer that absorbs? A sudden change of material reflects too, right at its edge.
A gentler layer must be thick and expensive. We need an absorber that light cannot see.
The trick, found in 1994 by Bérenger, and by Chew and Weedon, is to change not the material, but the coordinates.
Inside the border, let the position x pick up an imaginary part that grows with depth: x + (i/ω)∫σ dx.
A wave e^(ikx) at this complex position keeps its wavelength, but gains a factor e^(−(k/ω)∫σ dx): it dies away.
These are the same Maxwell equations in stretched coordinates, so the border matches perfectly: no echo, at any angle or frequency.
This is the perfectly matched layer, or PML. Side by side: the wall echoes, the lossy layer echoes, the PML stays silent.
On a grid, a tiny echo remains, so σ ramps up smoothly. Grazing and evanescent waves are the hardest to absorb.
In code, the whole method is four lines inside a time loop.
Update H from the curl of E. Update E from the curl of H. Absorb in the PML. Add the source.
Send in one short pulse, record what comes back, and a Fourier transform in time gives every wavelength from a single run.
For a Bragg mirror, a stack of alternating layers, the whole reflection spectrum lands right on the exact answer.
The price: every cell is updated at every step. A small 2D run takes seconds; a large 3D device, minutes to hours on GPUs.
And it sees what simpler models miss: on this fine glass relief, the thin-element model sends 96% of the light one way. FDTD, with shadows and light trapped in the ridges, finds 57%.
FDTD isn't exact either: it converges as cells shrink, curves become staircases, and the PML adds a small error.
But the core idea is simple. E updates H, and H updates E, one neighbour at a time.
A layer of complex-stretched space absorbs whatever leaves.
Now we can simulate almost anything. What we really want is the reverse: say what the light should do, and get the structure.
